steps.text: Lines one through four document the purpose of the file. This is a weighted k-nearest-neighbors imitation policy designed so every prediction remains inspectable.
Lines five through seven open a small wrapper function and enable strict JavaScript rules. The root parameter will later let the same policy attach safely to a browser.
The squaredDistance helper compares two sensor vectors. It subtracts matching features, squares each difference, and adds them, producing the distance used to rank demonstrations.
trainKnn receives demonstration rows and a default k of nine. These guard clauses reject an empty dataset or an invalid neighbor count before the model can make misleading predictions.
The counts object starts LEFT, STAY, and RIGHT at zero, then scans every row and increments the matching action. This becomes an inspectable class-balance receipt.
These weights give rarer action classes more influence. Dividing total rows by three class counts compensates for imbalance, while Math max prevents division by zero when a class is missing.
trainKnn now returns the model object. It preserves the original rows, k, and counts, then defines predict as the operation that turns a new sensor vector into a decision.
The prediction maps every demonstration to its action and squared distance, sorts from nearest to farthest, and slices out at most k rows. Math min also handles a dataset smaller than k.
Before voting, the model creates one empty bucket for each action: minus one for LEFT, zero for STAY, and one for RIGHT.
Each neighbor adds its class-balance weight divided by distance. Taking the square root restores ordinary Euclidean distance, and zero point zero two five keeps an exact match from dividing by zero.
The three raw votes are added into a total. Each vote is divided by that total to produce LEFT, STAY, and RIGHT probabilities; the fallback of one protects against an empty total.
The action array is sorted by probability, highest first. The first entry is the winning action that the agent will send back to the environment.

The decision receipt returns more than the winner. It includes probabilities, raw votes, the selected neighbors, and the nearest distance so the interface and a researcher can inspect why the action won.
These closing braces finish predict, the returned model object, and trainKnn. Training has produced one reusable and inspectable predictor.
The API object names the two public functions: squaredDistance for comparison and trainKnn for building the policy.
The final lines publish that API in two environments. Node receives module exports for automated tests, while the browser adds the same functions to AgentArcade before the wrapper closes.
